title: The thread pool
sub: Ready-made threads and a work queue
cards/0/body:
Creating a thread for every small task is expensive. The thread pool (ThreadPool) keeps a set of ready threads: tasks join a queue, and a free thread picks up the next one.

Task.Run, timers and continuations after await all run on the pool.
cards/1/task: Add 16 CPU tasks and start the clock. Watch the threads work through the queue.
cards/2/q: How many threads does the pool have at startup?
cards/2/options/0: Usually one per logical CPU core
cards/2/options/3: As many as there are queued tasks
cards/2/explain: By default the pool's minimum thread count equals the number of logical processors. From there the pool grows as needed.
cards/3/body: If every thread is busy and the queue is stuck, the pool adds a thread, but gradually, not all at once. Too many threads is bad too: they get in each other's way and eat memory.
cards/3/deep: The thread count is tuned by a hill-climbing algorithm: the pool tries adding or removing a thread and checks whether throughput went up. ThreadPool.SetMinThreads is a crutch that hides the problem instead of solving it.
cards/4/q: Why doesn't the pool create 1,000 threads right away for 1,000 tasks?
cards/4/options/0: Threads are expensive and there are few cores anyway: extra threads would just keep switching
cards/4/explain: On 8 cores, at most 8 threads run at once. The rest would burn time on switches and memory on stacks.
cards/5/q: What runs on the thread pool? Select all that apply.
cards/5/options/1: The continuation after await in a console app and ASP.NET Core
cards/5/options/3: Code on the WPF UI thread
cards/5/explain: The UI thread is a separate thread of its own. new Thread creates a new thread outside the pool.
cards/6/q: A pool task spends 10 minutes building a report. What's wrong with that?
cards/6/options/0: It ties up a pool thread for a long time; long tasks are better on a dedicated thread (TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning)
cards/6/options/2: The pool kills it after a minute
cards/6/explain: The pool is built for short tasks. A long one holds a thread, and the pool has to ramp up to compensate.
cards/7/pairs/0/1: A dedicated thread you create yourself
cards/7/pairs/1/1: Ready threads with a shared queue
cards/7/pairs/3/1: Runs one thread at any given moment
